title: The poor in spirit (Matthew 5:3)
hookLine: blessed are the poor in spirit: the empty-handed have room for the kingdom

lines: THE FIRST WORDS OF THE SERMON.
cards: Hashtag blessed. You've seen it under photos of a new car, a beach, a baby, a promotion. Blessed means things are going well.
Back on that hillside, crowds have followed Jesus from all over, bringing their sick. He has just sat down. And the first words of the sermon are a list of people who are blessed.
Only nobody on the list has a new car. It starts with the people who have nothing.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." This is the first of the Beatitudes.
Matthew's Greek word for blessed is makarios: happy, fortunate, well off, the word Greeks used for the gods and the rich. Its Hebrew counterpart opens the book of Psalms: blessed is the man.
So makarios is partly a congratulation. Lucky you. You're in a good place.
Then look who he congratulates. The Greek word for poor here isn't a little short this month.
It's the word for a beggar, someone with empty hands. Luke's version just says blessed be ye poor.

Matthew adds in spirit, and Christians read that in more than one way. Some hear the humble: people who know they can't earn their way to God. Others hear the poor who have no pride left to hold on to.
Some read both together. Either way, it's the opposite of self-sufficient. And the promise isn't someday.
Theirs is the kingdom of heaven: present tense. Here's a picture that helps. You can't receive a gift with your hands full.
Clutching your phone, your coffee and your bags, you have to put something down first.

teach.h: BLESSED ARE THE POOR IN SPIRIT.
teach.b: The poor in spirit already have their hands open. Maybe that's why this beatitude comes first. Everything else in the sermon is a gift, and empty hands can take it.

how: Some Christians know the Beatitudes by heart; Orthodox churches often sing them in the Divine Liturgy, and a number of churches read them on All Saints' Day.

o: rewarded by God for living a good, clean life
set apart and made holy by a priest's prayer
fortunate, well off: a word of congratulation

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: the Greek for blessed meant fortunate or well off
makarios: happy, fortunate, a word used of the gods and the rich.
Luke's version also says poor in spirit
Luke says blessed be ye poor. Matthew adds in spirit.
the promise of the first beatitude is only for the future
theirs is the kingdom of heaven: present tense.

games.q: a teacher sits down on a hillside and begins a sermon. who does he call blessed first?
games.why: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." it starts with the empty-handed.

practice: Rest your hands on your knees, palms open, facing up.
Quietly name one thing you can't do on your own right now, help you need and haven't asked for, something you can't fix; no shame in it, your open hands already say I don't have everything.
If you pray, you can bring that need to God with your hands open.

wordCard.voice: Blessed. Makarios in Greek: fortunate, well off, congratulations. And Jesus says it first to the poor in spirit.

orig.note: Greek: blessed, fortunate ones. the first word of each beatitude in Matthew 5.

carryVoice: Your line: empty hands can receive. The sermon starts with the empty-handed. Day two hundred thirty-three, done.
